body.heading: Lamps against the dark
paragraphs: Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, and some Buddhists, fills homes and streets with small oil lamps and candles, marking among other things the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil. Around the same season, Hanukkah’s candles grow by one each night for eight nights, commemorating an ancient rededication and a small jar of oil that lasted far beyond its measure.

In Sweden, Saint Lucia’s Day in mid-December brings processions of light into the darkest mornings of the northern year, led traditionally by a girl wearing a crown of candles — these days, safely, often electric ones.

body.heading: Why light, why then
paragraphs: It is not coincidence that these festivals cluster near the solstice in the northern hemisphere. When the days are shortest, communities answer together: we will make the light ourselves, and we will make it in company. The Lantern Festival closing Lunar New Year celebrations carries the same instinct into the first full moon of the year.
Light made alone is a lamp. Light made together is a message — to the dark, and to each other.

body.heading: Joining respectfully
paragraphs: If you are invited to share a festival that is not yours, go, accept what is offered, ask questions with appetite, and let your hosts lead. Most people are delighted to explain their celebrations to a genuinely interested guest.
And your own midwinter rituals — candles in a window, a walk to see the lights, one evening of lamps instead of screens — belong to the same old human project. Add your light to the season.

takeaway: When the days are shortest, the world’s answer is the same: make light, and make it together.
